kinds.d: Japanese soy sauces that differ by colour, saltiness, wheat share and brewing.

x.d: The standard Japanese soy sauce, roughly equal soybean and wheat, over 80% of domestic output and from the Kantō region.
Lighter-coloured and saltier shoyu made with amazake, popular in Kansai, about 14% of output.
Little or no wheat; darker, richer and more viscous, mainly made in Chūbu; wheat-free versions suit gluten avoiders.
Made with finished koikuchi in place of brine, giving a darker, stronger sauce; about 0.8% of output.

v.n: Suehiro Double Brewed Sashimi Soy Sauce

x.d: Mostly wheat with little soybean, pale and sweet, used in Kansai mainly for pickles; about 0.7% of output.

kinds.d: Fermented soybean paste with or without grain, in Japanese miso and Korean doenjang styles.

x.d: Dark grain-free soybean miso from Okazaki, Aichi, with a long maturing time and an astringent, umami flavour.
The most widely produced miso, mostly rice and barley with a little soybean, short-fermented, sweet and mild.
Rice (kome) miso, the common type in eastern Japan and Hokuriku; Shinshu is a named example.
Whitish barley miso from Kyushu, western Chūgoku and Shikoku, with a distinctive smell; a reddish version comes from northern Kantō.
Miso whose soybeans are mashed much more coarsely than in standard soy miso.
Korean paste mashed from meju bricks after the brine is drawn off as ganjang soy sauce.

kinds.d: A fermented paste of chilli, glutinous rice and soybeans used to season.

x.d: Regional gochujang from Sunchang County, noted in 18th-century texts and linked to Joseon palace cuisine.
x.dt: red chilli powder · glutinous rice · meju powder · salt

kinds.d: Sweet rice seasoning sold for cooking, hon-mirin and mirin-style seasoning.
Sake made or sold for cooking.
Japanese stock and its ingredients: kombu, katsuobushi, niboshi and instant dashi.

x.d: Dried kelp for dashi, sold by origin: Ma (Hakodate, mild and sweet), Rishiri (clean, for kaiseki), Rausu (rich), Hidaka (mild, cheapest).
Skipjack tuna simmered, smoked and mould-cured; graded arabushi, katsuobushi, karebushi and honkarebushi by repeated curing.
Small dried fish, mostly anchovies, for a strong dashi; heads and entrails removed to avoid bitterness.

kinds.d: Citrus-and-soy ponzu and dashi-based noodle tsuyu dipping sauces.
Dry seasoning sprinkled over rice: dried fish, sesame, seaweed, sugar, salt and often egg, shiso or salmon.

brands.d: Noda, Chiba soy sauce maker formed from eight family firms in 1917; world's largest shoyu producer.
Choshi, Chiba soy sauce and seasoning maker.
Shodoshima brewery of fifth-generation Yasuo Yamamoto, brewing in self-made kioke barrels; flagship Tsuru-bishio.

traditions.d: Yuasa claims to be the birthplace of Japanese soy sauce, with a soy sauce industry flourishing since the Edo period.
traditions.tech: koji fermentation of soybean and wheat with brine, pressed and aged
traditions.auth: Claim of origin is local and not settled

traditions.d: Natural brewing of soy sauce in handmade cedar-and-bamboo kioke barrels, about 1% of Japan's soy sauce.
traditions.tech: Tennen Jōzō Kioke Shikomi: natural wooden-barrel fermentation
traditions.mat: cedar and bamboo barrels, soybean, wheat, salt
traditions.auth: Brewed in kioke barrels; barrels can last over 100 years

traditions.d: Making, keeping and eating jang, the fermented sauces including soybean paste, soy sauce and red chilli paste.
traditions.tech: meju bricks fermented, brine drawn as ganjang, remainder mashed as doenjang
traditions.auth: Family transmission, mother to daughter, in earthenware jars

notes: Marukin, Yamasa products, San-J and Higashimaru kept as version names from old data only; Saikyo miso not found on retrieved pages and left out. Rishiri/Rausu/Ma from chefjacooks page.
